one_liner: Peer-reviewed AVX-512IFMA large-integer multiplication method, reported up to about 2.97x faster than GMP; no code released.
what_it_does: A research paper (Edamatsu and Takahashi, ICA3PP 2019, Springer LNCS) that vectorizes multi-precision integer multiplication with the AVX-512IFMA 52-bit multiply-add instructions and compares it with the same authors' earlier AVX-512F version and with GMP on a Cannon Lake CPU. No source, library or API has been published, so it is a design to reimplement, not something to link in place of GMP's mpz_mul/mpn_mul.
how_it_is_fast: AVX-512IFMA (VPMADD52LUQ / VPMADD52HUQ) multiplies 52-bit fields in each of eight 64-bit lanes and adds the low or high 52 bits of the product into a 64-bit accumulator. Storing operands in radix 2^52 leaves 12 spare bits per lane, so many partial products can be summed before any carry has to be propagated, and carry normalization is deferred. That gives eight 52x52-bit products per instruction instead of GMP's scalar 64x64-bit multiply-with-carry chain, and products wider than the 32x32-bit VPMULUDQ products an AVX-512F-only kernel is limited to. Whether it uses schoolbook, Karatsuba or Toom-style splitting is not documented in anything readable this session.
when_to_use: You are writing your own mpn-level multiply kernel for x86 cores with AVX-512IFMA (Cannon Lake, Ice Lake and later Intel parts that kept it, AMD Zen 4/5 per the record) and want a peer-reviewed design reference for radix-2^52 vector multiplication.
Sizing the payoff before adding an IFMA path to a bignum library: the paper's reported best case is about 2.97x over GMP and 3.07x over an AVX-512F implementation on one CPU.
Comparing against the authors' earlier AVX-512F (Knights Landing) design to see how much IFMA adds over a 32-bit-multiply vector kernel.
when_not_to_use: You need code you can run: nothing is published, so has_code is false and every number is the authors' own.
CPUs without AVX-512IFMA (anything before Cannon Lake/Ice Lake and later parts that dropped the extension): the technique cannot run there.
Very large operands where GMP switches to Toom-Cook or FFT multiplication: the operand-size range of the reported speedup is not documented, so it may not hold there.

Constant-time or cryptographic use: no side-channel properties are documented; for RSA-size modular work OpenSSL's IFMA almost-Montgomery routines (benchmarked in the VROOM sibling entry) are shipping code.
Decisions that need typical rather than best-case gains: both ratios are 'up to' figures.

integration.min_toolchain: not documented (needs a compiler with AVX-512IFMA intrinsics or assembler support)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX-512IFMA required; measured on a Cannon Lake processor (exact model not documented)

gotchas: Evidence is snippet only: the chapter (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-38991-8_5) could not be opened because link.springer.com and semanticscholar are egress-blocked, so GMP version, operand sizes, compiler, flags and exact CPU are unknown.
A radix-2^52 kernel needs conversion from and to GMP's 64-bit limbs (split and recombine passes); whether that cost is inside the reported times is not documented.
Cannon Lake, the test CPU, was a short-lived discontinued microarchitecture, so the ratios may differ on Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids or Zen 4/5.
No public repository is attributable: github.com/topics/avx512ifma lists no repositories, and Hibari-K's AVX-512F multiply repos (no IFMA variant, no license) are not linked to the authors.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Read it when designing a general (non-modular) IFMA multiply for single large operand pairs; for runnable code, DigitsOnTurbo patches GMP's multiplication (1.41x geomean at 512-32768 bits), lea-gl's truncated batch AVX-512 Montgomery code beats GMP 3.95-5.34x on batched modular products, and FLINT is the practical pick for very large sizes.
verified_claims_summary: Two search-engine summaries of the abstract (paper not opened) report large-integer multiplication with AVX-512IFMA up to about 3.07x faster than the authors' AVX-512F implementation and about 2.97x faster than GMP on a Cannon Lake processor. GMP version, operand sizes, compiler and flags are not documented.
status_note: A 2019 peer-reviewed paper with no released code or license, so it is reference material only; it could be re-tiered to B once a verifier can read the paper.
